claim: You cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user, and you cannot set a permissions boundary for the root user.
question: Can you attach an identity-based policy or a permissions boundary to the AWS account root user?

values.display: cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user
cannot set a permissions boundary for the root user

evidence.quote: The AWS account root user is affected by some policy types but not others. You cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user, and you cannot set the permissions boundary for the root user.

claim: In an account that is a member of an organization, the root user is affected by the SCPs and RCPs for that account, and a resource-based policy can name the root user as its principal.
question: Which policy types can limit or name the root user of a member account?

values.display: the root user is affected by the SCPs and RCPs
a resource-based policy can name the root user as its principal

qualifiers.scope: root user of a member account in AWS Organizations
qualifiers.condition: the account is a member of an organization

evidence.quote: However, you can specify the root user as the principal in a resource-based policy or an ACL. A root user is still the member of an account. If that account is a member of an organization in AWS Organizations, the root user is affected by SCPs and RCPs for the account.

claim: An SCP can specify a Condition element in allow and deny statements, and an SCP can use a NotAction element to exclude AWS services from the effect of the policy.
question: Can an SCP Allow statement carry a Condition element, and can an SCP use NotAction?

values.display: a Condition element in allow and deny statements
NotAction element to exclude AWS services

evidence.quote: You can specify a `Condition` element in allow and deny statements in an SCP.
The following example shows how you can use a `NotAction` element to exclude AWS services from the effect of the policy.

note: d040. FRESHNESS hypothesis (not verified here): full IAM policy language in SCPs since 2025-09; older material says an SCP Allow cannot carry a Condition. The changes lens owns the date.

claim: RCPs have no effect on resources in the management account of the organization.
question: Do resource control policies restrict resources in the management account?

values.display: no effect on resources in the management account
RCPs have no effect

evidence.quote: They have no effect on resources in the management account.

claim: The permissions of service-linked roles can't be restricted by RCPs.
question: Can an RCP restrict what a service-linked role does?

values.display: service-linked roles can't be restricted by RCPs
can't be restricted by RCPs

evidence.quote: The permissions of service-linked roles can't be restricted by RCPs.

claim: A user or role without any IAM permission policies has no access, even if an applicable RCP allows all services, all actions and all resources.
question: Does an RCP that allows everything give a principal any access on its own?

values.display: has no access, even if an applicable RCP allows all services
without any IAM permission policies has no access

evidence.quote: A user or role without any IAM permission policies has no access, even if an applicable RCP allows all services, all actions, and all resources.

claim: Scope iam:PassRole so that a user cannot pass a role that has more permissions than you want the user to have; you limit it to approved roles with the Resource element and to a service with the iam:PassedToService condition key.
question: Why does AWS require iam:PassRole and how do you scope it?

values.display: a role that has more permissions than you want the user to have
the iam:PassedToService condition key

qualifiers.scope: passing a role to an AWS service

evidence.quote: When setting the `PassRole` permission, you should make sure that a user doesn’t pass a role where the role has more permissions than you want the user to have.
The `iam:PassedToService` condition key can be used to specify the service principal of the service to which a role can be passed.

claim: PassRole is a permission, not an API call, so no CloudTrail logs are generated for IAM PassRole; you review the CloudTrail log of the call that created or modified the resource that received the role.
question: Does iam:PassRole appear as its own event in CloudTrail?

values.display: PassRole is a permission, not an API call
no CloudTrail logs are generated for IAM PassRole

evidence.quote: `PassRole` is not an API call. `PassRole` is a permission, meaning no CloudTrail logs are generated for IAM `PassRole`. To review what roles are passed to which AWS services in CloudTrail, you must review the CloudTrail log that created or modified the AWS resource receiving the role.

claim: Temporary credentials from AWS STS work globally, no matter which Region they come from.
question: Are STS temporary credentials limited to the Region of the endpoint that issued them?

values.display: work globally
no matter which Region they come from

evidence.quote: No matter which Region your credentials come from, they work globally.

claim: AssumeRoot returns short-term credentials for privileged tasks on a member account; only credentials from the management account or a delegated administrator account for IAM can call it, and root user credentials cannot make the call.
question: Who can call sts:AssumeRoot?

values.display: the management account or a delegated administrator account for IAM
root user credentials cannot make the call

qualifiers.condition: centralized root access enabled in AWS Organizations

evidence.quote: Returns a set of short term credentials you can use to perform privileged tasks on a member account in your organization. You must use credentials from an AWS Organizations management account or a delegated administrator account for IAM to call `AssumeRoot`. You cannot use root user credentials to make this call.

claim: An AssumeRoot privileged session lasts from 0 seconds up to a maximum of 900 seconds (15 minutes), which is also the default; a higher value makes the call fail.
question: How long can a privileged root session from AssumeRoot last?

values.display: 900 seconds (15 minutes)
a higher value makes the call fail

evidence.quote: The value can range from 0 seconds up to the maximum session duration of 900 seconds (15 minutes). If you specify a value higher than this setting, the operation fails.

claim: After you centralize root access, you can delete root user credentials (password, access keys, signing certificates, MFA) from member accounts, and new accounts created in AWS Organizations have no root user credentials by default.
question: What does centralized root access let you do with member-account root credentials?

values.display: delete root user credentials
new accounts created in AWS Organizations have no root user credentials by default

evidence.quote: After you centralize root access, you can choose to delete root user credentials from member accounts in your organization. You can remove the root user password, access keys, signing certificates, and deactivate multi-factor authentication (MFA). New accounts you create in AWS Organizations have no root user credentials by default.

claim: A privileged root session lets the management account or delegated administrator delete a misconfigured S3 bucket policy, delete a misconfigured SQS queue policy, and delete or re-enable root user credentials for a member account.
question: Which tasks can a privileged root session perform on a member account?

values.display: delete a misconfigured S3 bucket policy
delete a misconfigured SQS queue policy

evidence.quote: Once you launch a privileged session, you can delete a misconfigured Amazon S3 bucket policy, delete a misconfigured Amazon SQS queue policy, delete the root user credentials for a member account, and reenable root user credentials for a member account.

claim: AWS strongly recommends that you do not create access keys for the root user, because the root user has full access to all services and resources in the account, including billing information.
question: Should the root user have access keys?

values.display: do not create access keys for the root user
full access to all services and resources in the account, including billing information

evidence.quote: We strongly recommend that you do not create access keys for your root user because the root user has full access to all AWS services and resources in the account, including billing information.

claim: Some tasks can be performed only when you sign in as the root user; for example, if the only IAM administrator revokes their own permissions, you sign in as the root user to restore them.
question: Which situations require signing in as the root user?

values.display: can be performed only when you sign in as the root user
sign in as the root user to restore them

evidence.quote: However, you can perform the tasks listed below only when you sign in as the root user of an account.
If the only IAM administrator accidentally revokes their own permissions, you can sign in as the root user to edit policies and restore those permissions.

claim: A standalone account that is not part of AWS Organizations needs root credentials to update the email address, root user password and root user access keys, and to close the account; other settings such as account name and contacts don't require root credentials.
question: Which account settings need root credentials in a standalone account?

values.display: update the email address, root user password and root user access keys
to close the account

qualifiers.condition: the account is not part of AWS Organizations

evidence.quote: Standalone AWS accounts that are not part of AWS Organizations require root credentials to update the email address, root user password, and root user access keys. Other account settings, such as account name, contact information, alternate contacts, payment currency preference, and AWS Regions, don't require root user credentials.
Standalone AWS accounts that are not part of AWS Organizations require root credentials to close the account.
